languages.title: Fishing in Istria - The Best Fishing Tours, Waters & Seasons
languages.sub_title: Fishing in Istria - All Fishing Tours, Fishing Guides, Information, Closed Seasons & Minimum Sizes
languages.introduction:
The Istrian peninsula on the northern Adriatic is virtually surrounded by water and thus offers a true paradise for every angler. The region offers an impressive variety of fish species, diverse fishing methods in fresh and saltwater, and numerous opportunities for beginners and professionals.

Target Fish for Fishing in Istria - Numerous sought-after target fish are found in the waters around Istria. Particularly frequently caught are:

  • Sea bass (European sea bass)
  • Gilthead bream (Dorade)
  • Bluefin tuna
  • Mahi-mahi (Dolphin fish)
  • Bonito
  • Albacore
  • Mackerel
  • Grouper
  • Sea bream
  • Cuttlefish

These species are very popular with both coastal anglers trying their luck from the shore and deep-sea anglers, offering exciting fights and are also a real delicacy.

Successful Fishing Methods in Istria - Fishing methods in Istria are diverse and naturally vary depending on whether you prefer fishing from the shore or from a boat. Basically, in this section we have focused on the various fishing methods for sea fishing.

  • Spinning: Particularly effective for sea bass and mackerel.
  • Bottom fishing: For gilthead bream, bream and other bottom fish.
  • Jigging: For grouper and other predatory fish in deeper waters.
  • Paternoster rig: Ideal for fishing for various species simultaneously.
  • Big Game Fishing: Especially for tuna and other large fish from a boat.

Fishing Licenses Istria - A valid fishing license is required for fishing in Istria. This can be easily obtained online, in travel agencies or in local fishing shops. There are day, week and annual licenses. Prices vary depending on duration and type of fishing. For fishing for certain large fish such as tuna, an additional special permit is required. The license is valid throughout the Croatian sea area.
If you want to save yourself the stress, it is usually advisable to obtain the fishing license through a guide. Often the license is still valid if you want to go fishing yourself again after a guided tour.

Best Seasons for Fishing in Istria - Fishing in Istria is basically possible all year round. However, the best catches are achieved from spring to autumn. Summer and early autumn is the peak season for tuna, while sea bass and gilthead bream are particularly active in spring and late summer. Even in winter, the mild temperatures are attractive for freshwater fishing. Especially if you prefer to fish from the shore at sea, the months from October to April are recommended, as during this period the predatory fish move further into shallow water when it cools down somewhat over the winter months.

Guided Fishing Tours in Istria - Those who want to experience fishing in Istria in a particularly comfortable and successful way can book a guided fishing tour. Professional guides offer excursions for beginners and experienced anglers - from coastal fishing to big game fishing. The equipment and the necessary licenses are usually included in the price. A large selection of available tours and booking options can be found, as always, on our platform Catch A Guide, which specializes in fishing tours throughout Europe.

languages.introduction:
Die Region Norddalmatien rund um Städte wie Zadar und die vorgelagerten Inseln ist eine beliebte Region für Angler. Das kristallklare Wasser der Adria, zahlreiche Buchten der alten Fischerdörfer und eine abwechslungsreiche Unterwasserwelt mit einer vielzahl von Fangmöglichkeiten machen Norddalmatien zu einem beliebten Reiseziel für Angelfreunde aus ganz Europa.

Zielfische zum Angeln in Norddalmatien - In Norddalmatien erwartet Sie eine große Vielfalt an Zielfischen:

  • Seebarsch (Wolfsbarsch)
  • Dorade (Goldbrasse)
  • Blauflossen-Thunfisch
  • Mahi Mahi
  • Bonito
  • Albacore
  • Makrele
  • Zackenbarsch
  • Meerbrassen
  • Sepia

Diese Arten lassen sich sowohl vom Ufer als auch vom Boot aus fangen und bieten spannende Drills sowie kulinarische Genüsse.

Angelmethoden zum Angeln in Norddalmatien - Die beliebtesten Angelmethoden in Norddalmatien sind:

  • Spinnfischen: Für Wolfsbarsch, Makrele und Barrakuda sehr effektiv.
  • Grundangeln: Besonders für Dorade, Brassen und Meeräsche geeignet.
  • Brandungsangeln: An den langen Stränden der Region möglich.
  • Schleppangeln: Vom Boot aus auf Thunfisch und größere Meeresräuber.
  • Big Game Fishing: Für die Jagd auf Thunfisch und Schwertfisch in tieferen Gewässern.
  • Paternoster-Montage: Vielseitig für verschiedene Fischarten einsetzbar.

Angellizenzen fürs Angeln in Norddalmatien - Für das Angeln in Norddalmatien ist eine gültige Angellizenz erforderlich. Diese kann unkompliziert online oder vor Ort (z.B. in Angelläden, Touristenbüros oder bei der örtlichen Fischereibehörde) erworben werden. Kinder unter 14 Jahren dürfen mit einfachen Haken auch ohne Lizenz angeln. Es ist wichtig, sich vorab über die geltenden Vorschriften & Regeln vorab zu informieren und benötigte Lizenz stets mitzuführen, da bei Kontrollen empfindliche Strafen drohen können. 

Beste Jahreszeiten zum Angeln in Norddalmatien - Das Angeln ist in Norddalmatien das ganze Jahr über möglich. Die besten Fangergebnisse erzielen Sie jedoch:

  • Frühling und Herbst: Besonders aktiv sind Barsch, Meeräsche und Dorade.
  • Sommer und Herbst: Hochsaison für Thunfisch und Makrele.
  • Morgen- und Abendstunden gelten generell als beste Angelzeiten, um der Hitze zu entgehen und die Aktivität der Fische zu nutzen.

Geführte Angeltouren in Norddalmatien - Wer das Abenteuer auf dem Meer oder an den besten Spots von Nordalmatien erleben möchte, kann eine geführte Angeltour buchen. languages.introduction:
The Northern Dalmatian region, surrounding cities like Zadar and its offshore islands, is a popular destination for anglers. The crystal-clear waters of the Adriatic, numerous bays of old fishing villages, and a diverse underwater world with a multitude of fishing opportunities make Northern Dalmatia a favorite destination for fishing enthusiasts from all over Europe.

Target Fish for Fishing in Northern Dalmatia - In Northern Dalmatia, a wide variety of target fish awaits you:

  • Sea bass (European sea bass)
  • Gilthead bream (Dorade)
  • Bluefin tuna
  • Mahi-mahi (Dolphinfish)
  • Bonito
  • Albacore
  • Mackerel
  • Grouper
  • Sea bream
  • Cuttlefish

These species can be caught both from the shore and from a boat, offering exciting fights and culinary delights.

Fishing Methods in Northern Dalmatia - The most popular fishing methods in Northern Dalmatia are:

  • Spinning: Very effective for sea bass, mackerel, and barracuda.
  • Bottom fishing: Particularly suitable for gilthead bream, bream, and sea chub.
  • Surfcasting: Possible on the long beaches of the region.
  • Trolling: From a boat for tuna and larger predatory fish.
  • Big Game Fishing: For hunting tuna and swordfish in deeper waters.
  • Paternoster rig: Versatile for various fish species.

Fishing Licenses for Fishing in Northern Dalmatia - A valid fishing license is required for fishing in Northern Dalmatia. This can be easily obtained online or on-site (e.g., in fishing shops, tourist offices, or from the local fisheries authority). Children under 14 years of age are allowed to fish with simple hooks without a license. It is important to inform yourself in advance about the applicable regulations and rules and always carry the required license, as significant penalties can be imposed during inspections.

Best Seasons for Fishing in Northern Dalmatia - Fishing is possible in Northern Dalmatia all year round. However, you will achieve the best catches:

  • Spring and autumn: Sea bass, sea chub, and gilthead bream are particularly active.
  • Summer and autumn: High season for tuna and mackerel.
  • Morning and evening hours are generally considered the best fishing times to avoid the heat and take advantage of the fish's activity.

Guided Fishing Tours in Northern Dalmatia - Those who would like to experience the adventure on the sea or at the best spots can book a guided fishing tour. Professional guides offer excursions for beginners and professionals, including equipment and license. A large selection of available tours in Northern Dalmatia can be easily found and booked via the Catch A Guide platform, which specializes in fishing trips and guided tours in Croatia.

Dalmatien, die sonnenverwöhnte Küstenregion Kroatiens, gilt als wahres Eldorado für Angler. Die fischreichen Gewässer der Adria bieten eine beeindruckende Artenvielfalt. Zu den wichtigsten Zielfischen zählen Barsch, Meeräsche, Wolfsbarsch, Makrele, Dorade, Barrakuda und vor allem der begehrte Thunfisch. In tieferen Gewässern sind zudem Schwertfisch und gelegentlich sogar Haie zu fangen. 

Die besten Angelmethoden zum Angeln in Dalmatien - Die Angelmethoden sind so vielfältig wie die Landschaft: Küstenangler bevorzugen das Spinn- oder Grundangeln auf Wolfsbarsch und Meeräsche, während Bootsangler auf das Schleppangeln (Trolling) oder das klassische Hochseeangeln setzen, um Thunfisch und andere Großfische zu überlisten. Für Anfänger wie Profis gibt es zahlreiche Möglichkeiten, vom entspannten Uferangeln bis zum abenteuerlichen Big-Game-Fishing.

Angellizenz fürs Angeln in Dalmatien - Für das Angeln in Dalmatien ist eine Angellizenz zwingend erforderlich. Diese kann unkompliziert online oder bei lokalen Verkaufsstellen erworben werden. Beachten Sie, dass das Angeln an öffentlichen Stränden und in Häfen vom 1. Mai bis 1. Oktober verboten ist, ebenso wie in einigen Naturschutzgebieten.

Die beste Zeit zum Angeln in Dalmatien - Die besten Jahreszeiten zum Angeln richten sich nach Zielfisch und Methode. Besonders erfolgreich sind die Morgen- und Abendstunden. languages.introduction:
Dalmatia, the sun-drenched coastal region of Croatia, is considered a true angler's paradise. The fish-rich waters of the Adriatic offer an impressive variety of species. The most important target fish include perch, sea bream, sea bass, mackerel, sea bream, barracuda, and above all, the coveted tuna. In deeper waters, swordfish and occasionally even sharks can also be caught.

The best fishing methods in Dalmatia - The fishing methods are as diverse as the landscape: coastal anglers prefer spinning or bottom fishing for sea bass and sea bream, while boat anglers rely on trolling or classic deep-sea fishing to outsmart tuna and other large fish. For beginners and professionals alike, there are numerous possibilities, from relaxed shore fishing to adventurous big-game fishing.

Fishing license for fishing in Dalmatia - A fishing license is required for fishing in Dalmatia. This can be easily obtained online or from local retailers. The cost varies depending on the validity period, ranging from around 8 euros (1 day) to 40 euros (7 days). A valid ID must be presented upon purchase. Please note that fishing on public beaches and in harbors is prohibited from May 1st to October 1st, as is fishing in some nature reserves.

The best time to fish in Dalmatia - The best seasons for fishing depend on the target fish and method. The morning and evening hours are particularly successful. The main season for tuna extends from April to May and from July to November, with June excluded due to the spawning season. In summer, it is advisable to fish early or late in the day to avoid the heat and take advantage of the fish's activity.

Fishing tours in Dalmatia - Those who want to experience fishing in Dalmatia in a particularly comfortable and successful way can book a guided fishing tour. languages.title: Fishing in Lower Saxony – the best fishing tours, waters & seasons
languages.sub_title: Fishing in Lower Saxony: all fishing tours, guides, info, closed seasons & size limits
languages.introduction: If you are interested in fishing in Lower Saxony, this guide covers everything you need to know. Under certain conditions, it is possible to fish without a fishing license in Lower Saxony, for example at some coastal waters. The state offers numerous options—rivers, lakes, and the North Sea coast—where zander, pike, and perch are common targets. Popular waters include Steinhuder Meer, the Weser and Elbe rivers, as well as Dümmer See and streams in the Harz. Spring and autumn are generally considered the most productive seasons, while summer and winter call for specific techniques. Be sure to observe the applicable closed seasons and size limits to protect fish stocks; for example, pike is closed from 1 February to 15 April. Guided fishing tours are an excellent way to explore Lower Saxony’s waters. They are often led by experienced guides who show you prime spots and ensure all regulations are followed. Licenses are usually provided by the operator and often included in the tour. Whether you’re a beginner or experienced angler, you’ll find the right option here to build skills and enjoy nature.
languages.content:
Fishing in Lower Saxony without a license: Is it allowed?

In Lower Saxony, fishing without a license is indeed possible under certain circumstances. In coastal waters and so-called “free waters”, such as parts of the North Sea and some river sections, people aged 14+ may fish without a formal fishing license but must carry valid ID. However, most water authorities still require a license to issue a day ticket, so in practice this option is often limited to trout ponds. Note that even where a license is not generally required, all rules and regulations—such as closed seasons and minimum sizes—must be followed.

The benefits of guided fishing tours in Lower Saxony

Guided tours are very popular because the region offers a wide variety of waters—rivers, lakes and the North Sea coast—creating ideal conditions. The option to fish in coastal waters without a license also makes it easy for beginners to try the sport and enjoy nature. Lower Saxony is known for strong stocks of zander, perch and pike, which makes tours attractive for sport anglers. Plus, local guides share valuable know-how that helps improve skills and catch rates.

Lower Saxony fishing: The most popular waters for tours

Lower Saxony is a true angler’s paradise, with an impressive range of waters ideal for memorable trips. Favorites include Steinhuder Meer as well as the Weser and Elbe rivers—rich in zander, pike and perch—offering exciting challenges. Scenic canals and lakes like Dümmer See and the clear streams in the Harz also invite you to target trout and other species. This diversity of waters and fish makes the state a sought-after destination for anglers seeking nature and adventure.

Fishing license in Lower Saxony: Where to get it—is it included in tours?

You usually obtain a fishing ticket directly from water owners, clubs or tackle shops. For many inland waters, a fishing license is required to buy a ticket. On guided tours, tickets are often included in the price, but it’s best to confirm in advance whether the operator provides them or if you need to arrange your own.
languages.faq_title: Frequently asked questions about fishing in Lower Saxony
languages.fish_avail_intro:
Lower Saxony offers great opportunities to make the most of peak periods while observing closed seasons and size limits. Each season has its charm, with spring often particularly productive. To protect stocks sustainably, specific closed seasons exist for species like pike and zander, and minimum sizes ensure only sufficiently large fish are taken.

Best fishing seasons in Lower Saxony

- Spring (March–May): Often very productive as many fish—such as trout and zander—become active and prepare to spawn. Rising water temperatures increase bite frequency.
- Summer (June–August): Good for eel and catfish; the best times are often early morning or late evening when fish are most active.
- Autumn (September–November): Excellent for predators like pike and perch as they feed up for winter—prime time for bigger fish.
- Winter (December–February): Although bites are fewer, targeted trips for trout and other species can succeed. Cold months require specific techniques and patience, with chances for especially large fish.
languages.size_limit_intro:
- Pike minimum size: 40 cm, ensuring only adequately grown fish are harvested.
- Zander minimum size: 40 cm, to protect this popular predator stock.
languages.time_limit_intro:
- Pike closed season: 1 February–15 April.
- Zander closed season: 15 March–30 April.

The Franconian Switzerland region is renowned for outstanding fly fishing. Many tour providers—especially fly-fishing specialists—offer their trips on Catch A Guide. Spring and autumn are generally the best seasons to fish or book a tour in Bavaria, as most species can be targeted effectively then.

Lesser-known waters such as Blies, Prims and Nied also host many species. Typically, in addition to the whitefish common in Germany, you will find pike, perch, zander, eel, catfish, carp and more. languages.sub_title: Looking for a fishing tour, day trip or guided session in NRW? We’ve got you covered!
languages.introduction: In North Rhine–Westphalia, the variety of waters and species makes for diverse fishing and many tour options. For a successful trip you should know peak periods, closed seasons and size limits. Guided sessions offer strong advantages: guides know prime spots, handle permits and share valuable tips. This is especially helpful for beginners, as gear is usually provided. Popular waters include the Rhine, the Ruhr, Möhnesee and Biggesee. The best times vary by species: pike and zander in spring; eel and catfish in summer; perch in autumn; in winter, coarse fish like roach and bream. Key regulations include closed seasons and size limits. Pike may not be targeted from 15 Feb to 30 Apr; zander from 1 Apr to 31 May. Brown trout and similar species are closed 20 Oct to 15 Mar. Guided tours in NRW can be booked via platforms such as “Catch A Guide”, usually 5–6 hours and weather-dependent. A fishing license is normally required; beginner and group offers are available.
languages.content:
Fishing in NRW without a license: Is it allowed?

Fishing without a valid license is generally not permitted in NRW. Some limited exceptions exist (e.g., supervised youth), and a few clubs offer taster sessions under supervision, but these do not replace the official license.

Benefits of guided sessions in NRW

Guides know productive spots, advise on techniques and lures, arrange tickets and permits, and often unlock hard-to-reach waters—greatly improving your chances and overall experience.

Popular waters for tours in NRW

The Rhine (notably near Cologne and Düsseldorf), the Dortmund–Ems Canal and the Ruhr are rich in zander, pike and perch. Scenic reservoirs like Möhnesee are also excellent.

Species you can catch on guided trips

Common targets include zander, pike and perch in the Rhine and canals; trout in many lakes and streams; eel and carp in calmer waters.

languages.title: Fishing in Brandenburg – the best fishing tours, waters & seasons
languages.sub_title: All info about fishing in Brandenburg and about tours and guides.
languages.introduction: Brandenburg’s diverse waters are ideal for guided trips. The region includes the Spree, the Havel, numerous lakes and canals—home to eel, pike, perch, zander and carp; in clear waters, trout and grayling. Notably, fishing for coarse fish without a license is possible in Brandenburg, which makes it attractive for beginners. Pike anglers find excellent conditions, especially on the Havel and Spree. Guides take you to productive spots and know the most effective methods. They also assist with gear and with situations where license-free coarse fishing is allowed. Observe closed seasons and size limits: pike 1 Feb–31 Mar; zander 1 Apr–31 May; brown trout 16 Oct–15 Apr; grayling 1 Dec–31 May. Minimum sizes vary by species and water. Guided trips typically last 4–9 hours, can be booked online, and often offer specials for beginners and groups. Costs are usually €220–350 depending on duration and group size.
languages.content:
Fishing in Brandenburg: Waters, target species and special features

Anglers can expect variety: Spree, Havel, many lakes and canals with rich fish stocks. Targets include eel, pike, perch, zander and carp; in clear waters, trout and grayling. The option to fish for coarse species without a license makes Brandenburg attractive for newcomers and casual anglers.

Brandenburg: a paradise for pike tours

Numerous lakes, rivers and canals host strong pike populations—especially in the Havel and Spree. You can also target zander and perch. License-free coarse fishing lowers the entry barrier and lets you enjoy the region’s nature.

Benefits of hiring a guide in Brandenburg

Experienced guides know the best spots, techniques and lures, help with pike, zander and more, and share knowledge about local water ecology. The platform ""Catch a Guide"" provides a convenient way to find and book guides online.

Best fishing seasons in Brandenburg

- Summer: nocturnal species like eel and catfish fish well, especially in larger lakes and rivers.
- Autumn: excellent for predators feeding up before winter.
- Winter: coarse fish like roach and bream can still be targeted in deeper areas.

languages.title: Fishing in Baden-Württemberg – the best tours, waters & seasons
languages.sub_title: Fishing in Baden-Württemberg: guides, permits, tickets & closed seasons
languages.introduction: Baden-Württemberg offers varied fishing—DIY or guided. On Catch A Guide you can book trips on renowned waters such as the Rhine, Danube, Neckar and Lake Constance. These waters are known for their species mix: the Rhine holds zander, catfish and pike; the Danube offers roach and bream; the Neckar is noted for zander and catfish; Lake Constance attracts with pike and lake trout. A valid license is required unless you fish managed venues or small private waters. Species have specific closed seasons and minimum sizes: many are closed in spring (incl. pike and zander). In summer most species are open with few exceptions. In autumn, closures start for some salmonids and protected species like eel. In winter, certain salmonids and year-round protected fish remain closed. Guided trips typically last 6–8 hours, include tackle and instruction, and suit beginners and families. Costs are usually €200–300 per day; tours can be weather-dependent but run year-round.
languages.content: 1. Fishing in Baden-Württemberg: Tours & the most popular waters — The state is an angler’s paradise with the Rhine, Danube, Neckar and Lake Constance. The Rhine offers a wide range of species (zander, catfish, pike), the Danube’s varied current favors roach and bream, the Neckar provides accessible urban spots (e.g., Heidelberg, Stuttgart) with zander and catfish, and Lake Constance offers scenic pike and lake-trout fishing. Catch A Guide lets you browse and book tours easily via filters, maps, prices and photos. 2. Find your guide — Use Catch A Guide to search targeted guided trips across the region and book online. 3. Fishing without a license? — Generally not allowed in Baden-Württemberg; a fishing license is required. Exceptions include managed trout ponds and small private waters up to 0.25 ha under certain conditions.
languages.faq_title: Frequently asked questions about fishing in Baden-Württemberg
languages.fish_avail_intro: Prime season runs May–October, with May, June and September especially productive. Below is a quick species-by-species outlook.
languages.size_limit_intro:
Observe minimum sizes when fishing in Baden-Württemberg.
 
 - Species with closed seasons usually also have a minimum size.
 - Species without closed seasons often have no minimum size, though there are exceptions (e.g., carp).
 - Year-round protected species must not be targeted and have no minimum size.
 - Minimum sizes can vary locally—always check the specific water.
languages.time_limit_intro:
Closed seasons for popular species:
 
 - Spring is peak spawning for many species; therefore species such as zander, pike, brown trout and grayling are commonly closed.
 - In summer most species are open; year-round protected fish and a few exceptions (e.g., tench in some waters) may be closed.
 - Autumn is very productive for predators and coarse fish; closures begin for some salmonids and protected species such as eel.
 - In winter, most salmonids and year-round protected species remain closed.

languages.sub_title: Guided fishing in Rhineland-Palatinate: tours, closed seasons, size limits and waters
languages.introduction: Rhineland-Palatinate is an angler’s paradise: the Rhine, the Moselle and volcanic lakes such as Laacher See hold pike, zander, whitefish, carp and trout. Night fishing is permitted on many waters. Spring and autumn bring peak action, while eel and catfish are especially active in summer. Always observe closed seasons (e.g., for pike and zander) and minimum sizes. Guided trips by local experts include gear and insider knowledge and suit beginners and pros alike. Typical costs range from €150–300 per tour.
languages.content: 1. Waters, target species & highlights — The Rhine, Moselle and scenic volcanic lakes (e.g., Laacher See) are top venues; pike and whitefish are classic targets. Rivers in wine regions are great for fly fishing. Night fishing is allowed in many waters, opening extra opportunities for carp and more. 2. Why book a tour — Tours in Rhineland-Palatinate offer variety across rivers and lakes with many species (pike, zander, carp, trout). Night sessions are possible in many places and make for memorable experiences.

languages.title: Fishing in Schleswig-Holstein – the best tours, waters & seasons
languages.sub_title: All tours, guides and info on closed seasons, size limits and fishing in Schleswig-Holstein
languages.introduction: Schleswig-Holstein offers diverse fishing: coastal waters on the North and Baltic Seas plus inland waters such as the Schlei, Eider and Treene. Coastal targets include cod, flatfish, sea trout and herring; inland, pike, zander, perch, carp and eel. Guided trips provide gear and local knowledge for beginners and experienced anglers. Peak times vary: spring for herring; summer for eel and catfish; autumn favors predator fishing. Observe closures—e.g., pike (15 Feb–15 Apr) and zander (15 Mar–15 May)—and minimum sizes. A 28-day tourist license makes access easy for visitors without a full license.
languages.content:
All about fishing in Schleswig-Holstein & target species

Between two seas and with many inland waters, options abound. Baltic catch lists include garfish and mackerel at times. The Schlei is known for pike, with good chances for perch and zander. Licenses are generally required; tourists can obtain a 28-day license. Many waters also need a local day ticket. Spring herring runs draw crowds to Kappeln, Eckernförde and Flensburg’s harbor. Surf fishing along the Baltic, e.g., Schönhagen, is popular. Charter boats take you to prime North/Baltic grounds for larger fish.

Most popular waters for tours

The Baltic and North Sea host cod, mackerel and sea trout; inland, the Schlei and the rivers Treene and Eider provide pike, zander and perch. Scenic lakes round out the options.

Benefits of hiring a guide

Guides know productive spots and methods, help with permits and logistics, and let you focus on fishing. Catch A Guide is a convenient way to book online.

What to expect on the Baltic

Coastal fishing offers striking scenery and seasonal peaks—especially the March–April herring run. Shore and boat options are available. The tourist license enables 28 days of fishing without a full exam.

Fishing without a license?

Generally not allowed, with some exceptions: supervised trout ponds, the 28-day tourist license, and commercial charter boats where compliance is handled by staff.

Tourism license in Schleswig-Holstein

Thanks to many water types and species, the state is one of Germany’s best destinations for guided trips.

languages.title: Fishing in Saxony – the best tours, waters & seasons
languages.sub_title: All info on guides, tours, closed seasons and size limits for fishing in Saxony
languages.introduction: The eastern German states—including Saxony—are underrated for excellent fishing. Native predators (pike, perch, zander) are present in strong numbers and good sizes. Large waters such as the Elbe, Pöhl and Kriebstein fish very well for pike and zander. Guided trips are a great option for non-locals to learn waters, spots and methods from local experts. Typical ticket prices: ~€15/day and ~€50/week, depending on the water. Trout anglers do well in Saxon Switzerland. Prime seasons are early summer and autumn; for trout, early spring (March–April) is strong. Saxony is highly recommended if you haven’t fished here yet.
languages.content:
Fishing in Saxony: waters & target species overview

Saxony offers varied landscapes and waters. Top options include the Elbe, Mulde, Weiße Elster and the Kriebstein & Pöhl reservoirs. You can effectively target pike, zander, catfish, carp, eel and trout. A fishing license is required, plus a permit for the specific water (~€15/day, ~€50/week, available at tourist offices, tackle shops or online).

Guided tours in Saxony: where to book? 

Many local providers list guided trips on Catch A Guide—especially predator tours for pike, perch and zander. Guides know the waters well and can lead you to fish, significantly improving your success.

languages.title: Fishing in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern – best tours, waters & seasons
languages.sub_title: All info on guides, tours, closed seasons and size limits in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern
languages.introduction: Mecklenburg-Vorpommern is among Germany’s most popular fishing destinations. Beyond many freshwater options (large lakes and rivers) you can also fish the Baltic Sea and the famous Bodden lagoons. Expect big pike, zander and perch; along the coast, sea trout, garfish, mackerel and more. A tourist license can be purchased for all waters (fresh/salt) and replaces the usual federal license for 28 days; you still need the appropriate day tickets for each fishery. With so many species, there isn’t a single “best” season—good fishing is possible nearly year-round. Many Bodden guides list trips on Catch A Guide. Typical prices range from ~€200 to €600 depending on provider quality and boat equipment. It’s always worth the trip.
languages.content: 1) Guides & booking — ""Catch a Guide"" helps you book experienced local guides and discover the right techniques and spots for your target species. 2) Top waters & species — The Baltic, the Mecklenburg Lake District and numerous rivers/canals offer pike, zander, eel and more; coastal catches include cod, herring and sea trout. The 28-day tourist license lowers the entry barrier. 3) Fishing permits — Coastal waters require a coastal permit; inland waters require the relevant permission. Buy permits at tackle shops, tourist offices or online (e.g., via Fiskado). The tourist license costs ~€24 at many local offices or tourist centers. 4) Benefits of a guide — Expertise and local knowledge raise success and make the trip memorable. 5) Fishing without a license? — Generally not allowed, except with the tourist license; some trout ponds also allow supervised fishing without a license.

languages.title: Fishing in Limburg – best tours, waters & seasons
languages.sub_title: All about fishing tours in Limburg (NL): seasons, waters & more.
languages.introduction: In Limburg (Netherlands) you’ll find many waters and target species: rivers such as the Meuse (Maas) and Juliana Canal, plus lakes like the Maasplassen and Leukermeer. Coarse anglers can target bream, tench and carp; predator anglers can go for pike, zander, perch, catfish and even trout. The best periods are September–November and March & June. From 1 April until the last Saturday in May, the national predator closed season prohibits artificial lures. Hiring a local guide is a big advantage—they know techniques and hotspots. Typical tours run ~8 hours (multi-day options exist) and cost about €150–€350 depending on duration and group size. Gear is usually provided and trips are adapted to your skills; own boat by arrangement; beginners welcome. The VISpas is required—no German license needed. Always check local rules to avoid fines.
languages.content: Waters & species — The Meuse, Juliana Canal, Grensmaas, Roer, the Maasplassen and Leukermeer offer rivers, lakes and canals; even small border streams. Coarse species (bream, tench, roach, carp) and predators (pike, zander, perch, catfish, asp, eel and sometimes trout) are present. Many anglers from NRW visit Limburg because it’s close and very productive. Why a guide helps — High angling pressure means local knowledge matters. Guides who’ve fished here for decades know effective methods and areas and will boost your results.
languages.faq_title: Frequently asked questions about fishing in Limburg
languages.fish_avail_intro: Best overall: Sep–Nov. Also good: March and June (immediately before/after the predator closure). National predator closure: 1 Apr – last Saturday in May; artificial lures prohibited. For coarse fish, spring and summer are prime.
languages.size_limit_intro: Minimum sizes follow Dutch law and are not Limburg-specific. Some waters may have special harvest rules—check www.visplanner.nl.
languages.time_limit_intro: Dutch closed seasons apply nationwide. Predator closure: 01 Apr – last Saturday in May.

Inland you’ll target pike, zander, perch and coarse fish; around the IJsselmeer you can add eel; on the coast and in harbors, seabass, flatfish and mackerel appear seasonally. languages.title: Fishing in Southern Sweden / Götaland – best tours, waters & seasons
languages.sub_title: All about fishing in Southern Sweden: seasons, species, waters, tours & closures.
languages.introduction: Southern Sweden draws thousands of anglers each year. No German-style license is required, but you do need local day/week/month permits for the specific water or region. Surrounded by the Baltic and dotted with countless lakes and rivers, the area offers sea trout, salmon, mackerel and cod on the coast, and excellent pike, zander and perch inland. Big pike come from the large natural lakes; zander often from mid-water in those lakes. Top lakes include Vänern, Vättern, Bolmen and Åsnen. Productive regions include Skåne, Halland, Småland and Blekinge. The famous Mörrum is a marquee salmon river in the south. Catch A Guide lists many local guides.

languages.title: Fishing in Småland - the best fishing tours, waters & seasons
languages.sub_title: All info about fishing in Småland: season, species, waters, tours, closed seasons & more.
languages.introduction: The Småland region is one of the most popular destinations for anglers in southern Sweden. Famous lakes such as Bolmen, Åsnen, Rusken, Tiken and Möckeln are found here. Småland is known far beyond Sweden for its rich fish stocks. Most anglers come for pike, zander and perch, but there are also great opportunities for trout and salmon on the region's well-known rivers Mörrum and Emån. The Mörrum is one of Sweden's most famous salmon rivers with strong runs and great chances of success. For the best results on the big waters of this region, a guide is recommended—someone with a well-equipped boat who knows the best techniques and seasonal hotspots. The prime seasons in Småland are spring and autumn. In summer, higher water temperatures can create short bite windows—another reason to go with a guide. In winter you can try ice fishing, a style many anglers love and which is possible here.

languages.fish_avail_intro: The best seasons to fish Småland are late spring and autumn. Pike, perch and zander are most active from May to October.

languages.title: Fishing in Central Sweden / Svealand - the best fishing tours, waters & seasons
languages.sub_title: All info about fishing in Central Sweden: season, species, waters, tours, closed seasons & more.
languages.introduction: Central Sweden is an excellent fishing region with very diverse and extremely fish-rich waters. The most popular areas are Dalarna, Värmland, the Mälaren region and Stockholm. The large lakes Vänern, Vättern, Mälaren and Siljan, plus the well-known rivers Dalälven and Klarälven, offer unique opportunities for pike, zander, perch, salmon, sea trout, brown trout, grayling and more. Pike fishing peaks in spring and autumn, while zander and perch are best in the warmer summer months. Salmon, sea trout, trout and grayling are particularly productive from April/May to September. Central Sweden is also attractive because there are fewer anglers than in the south. You need a fishing card for most inland waters (not for coastal waters), available online or in local tackle shops. Day tickets seldom exceed €10 per angler. Booking an experienced guide is highly recommended; they offer trips on all major waters. More on tours and fishing in Central Sweden below.

languages.title: Fishing in Northern Sweden / Norrland - the best fishing tours, waters & seasons
languages.sub_title: All info about fishing in Northern Sweden: season, species, waters, tours, closed seasons & more.
languages.introduction: The farther north you go in Sweden, the wilder the landscape and fishing spots become. Zander are scarce in the north, but you can enjoy excellent fishing for trout, grayling, char, pike, perch, salmon and sea trout. Lapland is the best-known area, with unspoiled rivers and streams and stunning mountain lakes. Other good rivers for trout and grayling include Kalixälven, Torneälven, Piteälven and Vindelälven. In their estuaries, salmon and sea-trout fishing can also be very successful. Countless forest lakes with pike, perch, grayling and trout make this a top destination. Ice fishing is a special highlight in the remote northern regions. There are top-quality guided trips especially for trout, grayling and salmon. Everything about tours and fishing in Northern Sweden can be found below.

languages.title: Fishing on Madeira - the best fishing tours, waters & seasons
languages.sub_title: Everything about species, tours, waters and seasons for fishing on Madeira
languages.introduction: Madeira's location in the Atlantic makes it a hotspot for sea anglers. You can fish from shore, but offshore boat fishing clearly dominates. Blue & white marlin, tuna, swordfish, barracuda and mahi-mahi are among the targets. It's an El Dorado for boat anglers, though shore fishing is also possible in selected spots. Popular locations include Funchal Bay, Ponta do Sol on the southwest coast, and Paul do Mar on the west coast. Prime season runs May to October; thanks to the mild climate, fishing is possible year-round, with different species peaking in different months. Typical methods are bottom fishing and trolling—everything revolves around big-game fishing. Hiring a charter is strongly recommended. Prices vary widely: shared spots can start below €200 per angler per day, while a private boat often runs €600–1000. Catch A Guide offers a range of trips on Madeira for every budget.

languages.title: Fishing on the Azores - the best fishing tours, waters & seasons
languages.sub_title: Everything about guided tours, regulations, seasons & info for fishing on the Azores
languages.introduction: The Azores are an island group far off the European mainland. This unique location makes them a treasure for anglers. About 90% of fishing here is done by boat on the open sea. You can target blue & white marlin, various tuna species, swordfish, barracuda, grouper and many more. Angling generally splits into 'reef fishing' in nearshore areas and offshore fishing on seamounts or open water. Typical methods include big-game fishing, trolling, natural bait with whole sardines, and bottom fishing. Fishing is possible year-round. Prime tuna months are April to June, while marlin peak July to October. The Azores are known as one of the world's best marlin grounds, with average fish around 250 kg. DIY fishing is difficult—boat license and solid skills are required, otherwise success is unlikely. A fishing license is also mandatory. Local charters and guides listed on Catch A Guide take you to the best spots with the right gear and years of experience. Charter prices vary but commonly range from about €400–1200.
languages.faq_title: Frequently asked questions about fishing on the Azores

languages.introduction: The Algarve is Portugal's southern coastal region and a popular destination for anglers. Thanks to the mild climate, you can fish successfully all year. The focus is big-game fishing at sea for tuna, swordfish, bonito, sea bass and more. Hotspots include Lagos, Faro & Albufeira. Shore fishing for sea bass in the Algarve's shallow areas can also be very productive. For the best experience, book a local guide who will put you on fish with the right gear. You can book directly on Catch A Guide; they can also help arrange the mandatory fishing license. More information about tours and fishing in Portugal follows below.
languages.faq_title: Frequently asked questions about fishing in the Algarve

languages.title: Angeln in Berlin - die besten Angeltouren, Gewässer & Jahreszeiten
languages.sub_title: Alles was du zu Angelguidings und Angeltouren in Berlin wissen musst
languages.introduction: Trotz der dicht bebauten Stadt und der eher geringen Angelmöglichkeiten in der Stadt selber ist die Region ein wahres Paradies für Angler! Es gibt etliche Anbieter für Angeltouren in und um Zardar herum, die Thunfisch Angeltouren auf Top asugestatteten Booten anbieten. Die Saison zum Angeln in Zardar geht von Frühling bis Herbst, wobei der Sommer besonders gut liefert. Eine Angelkarte und robustes Angelgerät müssen zwingend gegeben sein. Bei einer Angeltour bzw. einem Angelcharter ist für alles gesorgt. Catch A Guide gibt einige Einblicke in das Angeln in Zardar und bietet einige Touren lokaler Anbieter direkt an.

languages.title: Fishing in Berlin – the best tours, waters & seasons
languages.sub_title: Everything you need to know about guided fishing and fishing tours in Berlin
languages.introduction: Despite its dense urban layout and fewer fishing options right in the city center, the Berlin region is a true angler’s paradise. With numerous rivers, lakes and canals, Berlin is among the largest connected inland fishing areas in Europe. The Spree, the Havel, and countless lakes such as Wannsee and Müggelsee invite anglers of all levels. Typical targets when fishing in Berlin are zander, perch, pike, eel, carp and trout, among many others. As everywhere, it’s important to follow the local closed seasons and minimum sizes for each species to avoid legal issues—these rules protect fish stocks and should be respected. Further down this page you’ll find details for Berlin’s closed seasons and minimum sizes. If you’re looking for a guided tour in Berlin, you’ll find many options on our site. Compare different trips and book directly online. There are tours tailored to many needs—Havel guidings, for example, are ideal for beginners and advanced anglers who want focused predator trips for zander, perch and pike. Family-friendly tours ensure fun and memorable experiences for all ages.

languages.title: Fishing in Roermond – the best tours, waters & seasons
languages.sub_title: Everything about species, tours, waters and seasons for fishing in Roermond
languages.introduction: Welcome to your ultimate guide to fishing and fishing tours in Roermond—one of the Netherlands’ most attractive angling areas. The city sits right on the River Meuse (Maas) and offers a maze of side arms, canals and the famous Maasplassen with incredible variety. Whether you’re after predators like zander, pike, asp and catfish, or coarse fish like carp and bream—Roermond has it all. Here you’ll find an overview of common species, effective methods and productive spots. Jigging soft baits is especially successful for zander and pike; spinning and natural baits such as worms or baitfish also work well. Pay special attention to Dutch closed seasons and minimum sizes (e.g., fixed closures for zander and pike), and make sure you have the proper permit. Exploring Roermond by boat is highly recommended—rent a fishing boat or join a guided tour to reach prime locations that are hard to access from shore. Use this guide to plan your Roermond trip and fish it successfully!
languages.content: Fishing in Roermond is a real highlight—well known in NRW and far beyond. The Meuse and connected waters suit predators and coarse fish alike. Common catches include: • Perch—often schooling close to the bank • Zander—very active at dusk along edges and drops in the river and canals • Pike—frequent in shallows near reed and lilies • Asp—hard-fighting in current • Catfish—mostly in deeper river sections • Carp—found nearly everywhere in river, canals and plassen. Jigging soft baits is most productive; deadbaiting works well for pike and zander; perch take aggressive lures and worms. Boat rental options are plentiful and provide access to the best spots.

languages.title: Fishing in Hamburg – the best tours, waters & seasons
languages.sub_title: See, compare and book fishing guides in Hamburg
languages.introduction: If you’re interested in guided fishing in Hamburg, here’s everything you need to know to prepare. A local guide does more than show techniques and lures—you’ll also gain access to prime Elbe spots that are hard to locate without local knowledge. Hamburg—often called Germany’s “zander capital”—offers a unique urban backdrop of canals, river sections and harbor basins. Besides zander you can catch pike and perch while enjoying the city skyline. Note the rules: for example, closed season for zander and pike runs 1 February–31 May, and there are both minimum and maximum sizes (“harvest windows”) for certain species. You’ll need a valid fishing license or, when fishing with a licensed guide, the required local levy. Prime months are March–May and September–November; winter can also be rewarding for larger fish. Most guides supply quality tackle, so you don’t need to bring rods, reels or lures. Whether beginner or experienced, a Hamburg tour is a great way to optimize your success and enjoy the city’s scenery.
languages.content:
Guides in Hamburg – benefits: Personal instruction, local hotspots, transferable lure/tactic knowledge and an authentic experience on the Elbe.

Fishing Hamburg – local expertise matters: Rich species diversity and varied water types reward those who follow local licensing and regulations.

Why tours in Hamburg are so popular: As Germany’s “zander capital,” Hamburg’s network of canals, rivers and harbor basins holds strong zander, plus perch and pike. Boat fishing while viewing the skyline is a highlight. Experienced guides share tactics that raise success for all skill levels.

Seasons & notes: see season overview below and observe closed seasons and size windows.
languages.faq_title: Frequently asked questions about fishing in Hamburg
languages.fish_avail_intro:
Hamburg is a pioneer in German recreational fisheries with its harvest-window system defining both minimum and maximum sizes to protect juveniles and prime spawners. Closed seasons also apply to certain species during their spawning periods.

Best times:
• Spring (Mar–May): strong for coarse fish
• Summer (Jun–Aug): June is peak for zander; eel and catfish active in warm water
• Autumn (Sep–Nov): excellent for pike, perch, zander
• Winter (Dec–Feb): fewer bites but chance of larger fish
languages.size_limit_intro: Hamburg uses harvest windows (min & max) to protect stocks. Pike: min 45 cm, max 75 cm. Zander: min 45 cm, max 75 cm. Sea trout: 40–65 cm; max two fish/day.
languages.time_limit_intro: Closed season for pike and zander: 1 February–31 May (no artificial baits or baitfish allowed during this time). Eel: closed 1 November–31 …

The Weser runs through Bremen and provides popular hotspots with outstanding zander and pike sessions. Water types vary from rivers to lakes and gravel pits. Main rivers are the Weser, Wümme and Lesum. Popular lakes like Werdersee and Unisee hold carp, tench and whitefish. There are also many small ditches and canals worth exploring. As everywhere, respect closed seasons and minimum sizes. In Bremen, zander and pike are closed 1 February–15 May. More details on seasons and sizes can be found below. For guided tours there are many offers on our platform—compare and book online. Weser guidings suit beginners and advanced anglers focused on predators (zander, perch, pike). Family-friendly trips ensure fun and memorable experiences for all ages.

languages.introduction: Rotterdam offers a unique urban fishing experience known as street fishing. Rivers, canals and harbor basins create a paradise for predator, coarse and even brackish-water anglers. For predator fans, the city waters hold strong zander, aggressive perch and powerful pike. Bridges, quays and harbor structures are prime ambush points. Coarse anglers also do well with bream, roach and carp in calmer canals and basins. A special feature is brackish water in the port area, which attracts salt-water predators like European seabass. The Nieuwe Maas and harbor basins provide excellent chances for these sought-after fish. You may also encounter mullet, garfish and occasionally mackerel. This diversity makes fishing in Rotterdam exciting—you never know what the next cast brings. Street fishing blends urban flair with a nature-close experience—just be sure to check local permits and regulations for responsible angling.

The region of Dutch “trophy-fish waters” draws anglers to Hollands Diep, Haringvliet and Volkerak—venues for many tournaments. As mentioned, the main targets here are pike, perch & zander.

languages.title: Angeln in Schweden
languages.sub_title: Alle Infos zum Angeln in Schweden: Angelsaison, Fischarten, Gewässer, Angeltouren, Angelreisen und Camps
languages.introduction: Schweden fischt sich von Süden nach Norden wie zwei verschiedene Länder. Im Süden liegen nährstoffreiche Flachseen mit Schilfkanten und Krautfeldern, in denen Hecht, Zander und Barsch stehen. Im Norden fließen kalte, klare Flüsse durch Nadelwald, dazu kommen Bergseen über der Waldgrenze — dort geht es um Äsche, Bachforelle und Saibling. Dazwischen liegen die großen Seen Vänern, Vättern, Mälaren und Hjälmaren, die beides bedienen. Die Küste ist ein eigenes Kapitel. An der Westküste zwischen Öresund und Bohuslän wird watend auf Meerforelle gefischt, an der Ostsee reicht der Salzgehalt so weit herunter, dass Hecht und Barsch bis weit in die Schären hinaus vorkommen. In Brackwassergebieten wie den Stockholmer Schären lassen sich an einem Tag Süß- und Salzwasserfische fangen. Ein verbreitetes Missverständnis betrifft das Jedermannsrecht: Allemansrätten regelt Betreten und Übernachten, nicht das Angeln. Kostenfrei mit Handgerät fischen darfst du an der gesamten Küste sowie auf Vänern, Vättern, Mälaren, Hjälmaren und Storsjön. An den meisten übrigen Binnengewässern brauchst du ein Fiskekort des zuständigen Fischereivereins — meist günstig, tageweise oder für die Woche, online oder im Ort erhältlich. Die Saison läuft im Grunde ganzjährig, nur mit sehr unterschiedlichen Inhalten. Von Februar bis in den April trägt das Eis in Värmland, Dalarna und weiter nördlich; ab Mai öffnen die Fließgewässer; im Juni und Juli wird es im Norden kaum dunkel; September bis November sind die stärksten Wochen auf Großhecht. Für Angler aus Deutschland ist die Anreise überschaubar. Südschweden erreichst du über die Fähren nach Trelleborg oder über Dänemark und die Öresundbrücke an einem Tag. Nach Mittelschweden sind es weitere fünf bis sechs Fahrstunden, nach Lappland deutlich mehr — dort lohnt sich der Flug nach Luleå oder Kiruna.
languages.content:
Die wichtigsten Reviere

Småland und Blekinge gelten als Raubfischland. Åsnen, Bolmen, Möckeln und der Mien sind flache bis mitteltiefe Seen mit klaren Strukturkanten, in denen Hecht regelmäßig Meterlänge erreicht und Zander gute Bestände hat. Kleinere Flüsse wie die Ronnebyån lassen sich vom Kajak oder Bellyboat befischen. Der Mälaren und die Stockholmer Schären liegen direkt nebeneinander und funktionieren völlig unterschiedlich: im See tiefe Rinnen und Zanderplätze, draußen in den Schären flache Buchten mit Hecht im Brackwasser. Der Vättern ist wesentlich tiefer und klarer, mit Bestand an Seesaibling und Seeforelle. Dalarna und Värmland sind Fliegenfischerregionen. Die Flüsse um Älvdalen führen Äsche und Bachforelle, gefischt wird watend mit Trockenfliege oder Nymphe. Im Winter kommt Eisangeln auf Saibling dazu. Nordschweden und Lappland bieten Wildnisangeln mit langen Anfahrten: Saibling und Forelle in Bergseen, Lachs in den großen Küstenflüssen, dazu Äsche in fast jedem Fließgewässer. Die Westküste ist Meerforellenrevier. Gefischt wird vom Ufer über Blasentang und Steinfeldern, mit Spinnrute oder Zweihandrute.

 

Zielfische und Saison

Hecht steht ganzjährig zur Verfügung, mit klaren Spitzen im Frühjahr nach dem Laichen und im Spätherbst. Zander läuft von Juni bis Oktober und beißt oft erst in der Dämmerung. Barsch ist die verlässlichste Art über die gesamte offene Saison. Äsche und Bachforelle haben ein enges Fenster von etwa Ende Mai bis September, abhängig von Wasserstand und Schneeschmelze. Lachs steigt von Juni bis August in die Flüsse. Meerforelle wird an der Küste vor allem im Frühjahr und Herbst gefangen, in milden Wintern auch dazwischen.

 

Methoden und Ausrüstung

Spinnfischen dominiert auf Raubfisch, vom Ufer wie vom Boot; Gummiköder und flachlaufende Wobbler decken die meisten Situationen ab. Trolling ist auf den großen Seen üblich, Vertikalangeln auf Zander in tieferen Rinnen. In den Flüssen des Nordens ist Fliegenfischen die Standardmethode, meist Klasse 4 bis 6 auf Äsche und Forelle, deutlich schwerer auf Lachs und Hecht. Fürs Eisangeln reichen Kurzrute, Bohrer und Pilker — kalte Kleidung vorausgesetzt.

 

Regeln, die du kennen solltest

Neben dem Fiskekort gelten regional Mindestmaße, Schonzeiten und Entnahmebegrenzungen, vor allem für Lachs, Meerforelle und für Hecht in Küstennähe. Widerhakenlose Haken und Fangbeschränkungen sind an vielen Lachsstrecken vorgeschrieben. Die Regeln unterscheiden sich je Län und ändern sich, ein Blick auf die Seite des jeweiligen Fischereivereins vor der Reise ist Pflicht. 

 

Geführte Angeltouren und Angelreisen oder Angelulaub auf eigene Faust

Wer die Reviere nicht kennt, spart mit einem Guide vor allem Zeit: Ein Tag auf dem Wasser mit jemandem, der die Kanten und die Saisonmuster kennt, ersetzt oft mehrere eigene Erkundungstage. Auf Catch A Guide findest du für Schweden geführte Tagestouren, Angelcamps mit eigenem Boot am Steg für alle, die selbst planen wollen, sowie mehrtägige Angelreisen mit Unterkunft und Programm.

languages.title: Fishing in Sweden
languages.sub_title: Everything you need to know about fishing in Sweden: season, species, waters, guided tours, fishing trips and camps
languages.introduction: Sweden fishes like two different countries from south to north. The south has nutrient-rich shallow lakes with reed edges and weed beds, holding pike, zander and perch. In the north, cold, clear rivers run through pine forest, joined by mountain lakes above the treeline — up there it's about grayling, brown trout and Arctic char. In between sit the big lakes Vänern, Vättern, Mälaren and Hjälmaren, which serve both. The coast is a chapter of its own. Along the west coast between the Öresund and Bohuslän, anglers wade for sea trout, while the Baltic is brackish enough that pike and perch occur far out into the archipelagos. In brackish areas such as the Stockholm archipelago, you can catch freshwater and saltwater species on the same day. One common misunderstanding concerns the Right of Public Access: Allemansrätten covers walking and camping, not fishing. You can fish free of charge with handheld tackle along the entire coast and on Vänern, Vättern, Mälaren, Hjälmaren and Storsjön. On most other inland waters you need a fiskekort from the local fishing association — usually inexpensive, available by the day or the week, online or locally. The season effectively runs year-round, but with very different content. From February into April the ice holds in Värmland, Dalarna and further north; the rivers open from May; in June and July it barely gets dark in the north; September to November are the strongest weeks for big pike. For anglers from Germany, getting there is manageable. Southern Sweden is a one-day drive via the ferries to Trelleborg or through Denmark and across the Öresund Bridge. Central Sweden is another five to six hours; Lapland considerably more — for that, a flight to Luleå or Kiruna makes sense.
languages.content:
The main regions

Småland and Blekinge are predator country. Åsnen, Bolmen, Möckeln and Lake Mien are shallow to medium-depth lakes with well-defined structure, where pike regularly reach the metre mark and zander stocks are good. Smaller rivers such as the Ronnebyån can be fished from a kayak or belly boat. Lake Mälaren and the Stockholm archipelago sit side by side and work in completely different ways: deep channels and zander spots in the lake, shallow brackish bays with pike out in the archipelago. Vättern is far deeper and clearer, holding Arctic char and lake trout. Dalarna and Värmland are fly fishing regions. The rivers around Älvdalen carry grayling and brown trout, fished by wading with dry fly or nymph. In winter, ice fishing for char is added. Northern Sweden and Lapland offer wilderness fishing with long drives: char and trout in mountain lakes, salmon in the major coastal rivers, and grayling in almost every running water. The west coast is sea trout territory, fished from shore over bladderwrack and boulder fields with spinning rod or two-handed rod.

 

Target species and season

Pike is available year-round, with clear peaks in spring after spawning and in late autumn. Zander runs from June to October and often only feeds at dusk. Perch is the most reliable species across the whole open season. Grayling and brown trout have a narrow window from roughly late May to September, depending on water levels and snowmelt. Salmon runs into the rivers from June to August. Sea trout is caught along the coast mainly in spring and autumn, and in mild winters in between as well.

 

Methods and tackle

Spin fishing dominates for predators, from shore and from the boat; soft plastics and shallow-running crankbaits cover most situations. Trolling is standard on the big lakes, vertical jigging for zander in deeper channels. In the northern rivers, fly fishing is the default method — usually 4- to 6-weight for grayling and trout, considerably heavier for salmon and pike. For ice fishing, a short rod, an auger and jigging lures are enough, assuming cold-weather clothing.

 

Rules you should know

Alongside the fiskekort, regional minimum sizes, closed seasons and bag limits apply, particularly for salmon, sea trout and for pike close to the coast. Barbless hooks and catch limits are mandatory on many salmon beats. Rules differ by county and do change, so checking the relevant fishing association's website before you travel is essential.

 

Guided tours and fishing trips, or a fishing holiday on your own terms

If you don't know the waters, a guide mainly saves you time: a day on the water with someone who knows the edges and the seasonal patterns often replaces several days of scouting on your own. On Catch A Guide you'll find guided day trips in Sweden, fishing camps with your own boat at the dock for those who prefer to plan their own days, and multi-day fishing trips with accommodation and a set programme.
languages.faq_title: Frequently asked questions about fishing in Sweden

languages.title: Angeln in Norwegen
languages.sub_title: Alle Infos zum Angeln in Norwegen: Angelsaison, Fischarten, Fjorde und Flüsse, Angeltouren, Angelreisen und Camps
languages.introduction: Mit allen Fjorden und Inseln misst Norwegens Küstenlinie über 100.000 Kilometer. Dahinter beginnt ein Land, das zu weiten Teilen aus Fels, Hochebene und Wasser besteht — rund 450.000 Seen sind kartiert, dazu tausende Flüsse. Angeltechnisch bedeutet das zwei getrennte Welten, die sich nur an den Flussmündungen berühren: das Meer mit Dorsch, Köhler, Heilbutt und Leng, und das Süßwasser mit Forelle, Saibling, Äsche und Lachs. Der Norden trägt den Ruf des Landes. Vor Lofoten, Sørøya und der Finnmark fällt der Grund direkt vor der Küste steil ab, sodass Tiefen von 100 bis 300 Metern in kurzer Bootsfahrt erreichbar sind — der Grund, warum sich dort die meisten Angelcamps konzentrieren. Im Süden und Westen ist das Bild anderes: geschütztere Fjorde, kleinere Boote, mehr Uferangeln auf Meerforelle, Pollack und Makrele. Ein Unterschied zu fast allen anderen europäischen Zielen betrifft die Kosten. Das Angeln im Meer ist in Norwegen für jeden kostenfrei und ohne Lizenz möglich. Im Süßwasser brauchst du ein Fiskekort, das je nach Gewässer meist zwischen 5 und 25 Euro pro Tag liegt. Die Ausnahme sind die klassischen Lachsflüsse — dort kosten gute Strecken in der Hauptzeit ein Vielfaches, und die begehrten Wochen sind Jahre im Voraus vergeben. Die Saison folgt der Breite. In Südnorwegen läuft die Hauptzeit von Mai bis September. Im Norden kommt mit dem Skrei zwischen Januar und April ein eigenes Fenster dazu, während der Sommer dort unter der Mitternachtssonne rund um die Uhr befischbar ist. Wetter bleibt der bestimmende Faktor: An exponierten Küsten fallen Ausfahrten regelmäßig aus, und wer im Winter anreist, sollte Pufferzeit einplanen. Für Angler aus Deutschland ist Südnorwegen per Fähre ab Kiel oder Hirtshals in einer Nacht erreichbar. Nach Lofoten sind es rund 2.000 Straßenkilometer — dort ist der Flug nach Bodø, Evenes oder Tromsø die übliche Variante.
languages.content:
Die wichtigsten Angelreviere in Norwegen

Südnorwegen und der Oslofjord sind das Einsteigerrevier mit der kürzesten Anreise. An der Küste zwischen Oslo und der schwedischen Grenze, etwa bei Fredrikstad, wird vom Ufer und aus flachen Booten auf Meerforelle gefischt, dazu kommen Makrele, Pollack und Hornhecht als Beifang. Der Dorschbestand im Oslofjord ist seit Jahren stark eingebrochen; viele Anbieter fischen dort bewusst nicht gezielt auf Dorsch. Im Binnenland liegen mit der Glomma bei Rånåsfoss und den Seen um Lillestrøm gute Raubfischgewässer mit Hecht, Barsch, Zander und Rapfen. Westnorwegen zwischen Stavanger und Ålesund ist Fjordangeln im engeren Sinn: steile Wände, tiefes Wasser dicht am Ufer, Köhler und Pollack als Standardfische. Die Fjorde sind windgeschützter als die offene Küste, was die Ausfalltage reduziert. Trøndelag mit Hitra und Frøya verbindet beides. Vor den Inseln steht Heilbutt auf den Sandbänken, im Landesinneren fließen mit Gaula, Orkla und Namsen einige der bekanntesten Lachsflüsse Europas. Nordland und die Lofoten sind das dichteste Camp-Gebiet des Landes. Die Kombination aus geschützten Sunden und steilen Kanten erlaubt auch bei schlechtem Wetter Ausfahrten, und zwischen Januar und April zieht der Skrei — laichreifer Wanderdorsch aus der Barentssee — an die Küste. Troms und Finnmark bilden das Extrem: Sørøya, Havøysund und die Küste bis zur russischen Grenze bringen die größten Heilbutte und Köhler. Dafür sind Anreise und Wetterrisiko am höchsten.

 

Zielfische und Saison

Dorsch lässt sich ganzjährig fangen, mit der Spitze zur Skrei-Saison von Januar bis April im Norden. Köhler beißt am kräftigsten von Juni bis September, wenn die Schwärme im Freiwasser stehen. Heilbutt hat sein Fenster ungefähr von Mai bis Oktober, mit den besten Wochen im Spätsommer. Leng und Lumb stehen tiefer und werden ganzjährig gefangen, vorwiegend im Frühjahr. Makrele erscheint an der Südküste ab Juni. Lachs steigt zwischen Juni und August in die Flüsse, Meerforelle wird an der Küste vor allem im Frühjahr und Herbst befischt, Forelle und Saibling in den Gebirgsseen von Juni bis September, sobald die Schneeschmelze durch ist.

 

Methoden und Ausrüstung

Im Meer dominiert das Pilken und Jiggen über tiefem Wasser, meist mit 150 bis 400 Gramm, an Strömungskanten auch schwerer. Auf Heilbutt wird mit Naturköder am Grund oder mit großen Gummifischen im Drift gefischt, häufig über Sandflächen zwischen 30 und 80 Metern. Geflochtene Schnur ist wegen der Tiefe Standard. An der Küste reichen für Meerforelle Spinnrute und Watkleidung; in den Lachsflüssen wird überwiegend mit der Zweihandrute gefischt. Für die Gebirgsseen genügt leichtes Gerät der Klasse 4 bis 6.

 

Regeln, die du kennen solltest

Drei Punkte sind für Norwegen-Reisende zentral. Erstens die Ausfuhrmenge: Fischfilet darf nur begrenzt ausgeführt werden, wobei Gäste registrierter Betriebe eine höhere Menge mitnehmen dürfen als Selbstversorger. Für Heilbutt gelten gesonderte Regeln. Zweitens die Desinfektionspflicht: Gebrauchtes Angelgerät, Watstiefel und Boote aus dem Ausland müssen vor dem Einsatz in Lachsführenden Gewässern desinfiziert und mit Nachweis versehen werden. Hintergrund ist der Parasit Gyrodactylus salaris. Drittens die Lizenzen im Süßwasser: Neben dem lokalen Fiskekort ist für Lachs, Meerforelle und Wanderseesaibling zusätzlich die staatliche Fischereiabgabe fällig. Mindestmaße, Schonzeiten und Quoten variieren je Fluss und Region, und einzelne Lachsflüsse werden bei schwachen Aufstiegszahlen kurzfristig gesperrt. 

 

Geführte Angeltouren und Angelurlaub

Wer in Norwegen zum ersten Mal aufs Meer fährt, unterschätzt meist zwei Dinge: die Tiefe und die Streuung der Fische. Ein Guide mit Echolot und Ortskenntnis kürzt die Suche erheblich ab, gerade auf Heilbutt. Auf Catch A Guide findest du geführte Tagestouren, Angelcamps mit Boot und Filetierhaus für alle, die selbst hinausfahren wollen, sowie mehrtägige Angelreisen mit Unterkunft und Programm. Für Lofoten und die Finnmark gilt: Die besten Camps sind oft ein Jahr im Voraus ausgebucht.

languages.title: Fishing in Norway
languages.sub_title: Everything you need to know about fishing in Norway: season, species, fjords and rivers, guided tours, fishing trips and camps
languages.introduction: Counting every fjord and island, Norway's coastline runs to more than 100,000 kilometres. Behind it lies a country made largely of rock, plateau and water — around 450,000 lakes are mapped, along with thousands of rivers. In fishing terms that means two separate worlds, meeting only at the river mouths: the sea, with cod, coalfish, halibut and ling, and freshwater, with trout, char, grayling and salmon. The north carries the country's reputation. Off Lofoten, Sørøya and Finnmark the seabed drops steeply just offshore, putting depths of 100 to 300 metres within a short boat ride — which is why most fishing camps are concentrated there. The south and west look different: more sheltered fjords, smaller boats, and more shore fishing for sea trout, pollack and mackerel. One point sets Norway apart from almost every other European destination: cost. Sea fishing is free for everyone and requires no licence. In freshwater you need a fiskekort, usually between 5 and 25 euros per day depending on the water. The exception is the classic salmon rivers, where good beats in the peak weeks cost many times that, and the sought-after slots are booked years in advance. The season follows the latitude. In southern Norway the main period runs from May to September. In the north, the skrei adds a window of its own between January and April, while summer up there can be fished around the clock under the midnight sun. Weather remains the deciding factor: on exposed coasts trips are regularly cancelled, and anyone travelling in winter should build in spare days. From Germany, southern Norway is an overnight ferry from Kiel or Hirtshals. Lofoten is around 2,000 road kilometres away — most anglers fly to Bodø, Evenes or Tromsø instead.
languages.content:
The main regions

Southern Norway and the Oslofjord are the entry-level option with the shortest journey. Along the coast between Oslo and the Swedish border, around Fredrikstad, sea trout are fished from shore and from small boats, with mackerel, pollack and garfish as by-catch. Cod stocks in the Oslofjord have collapsed in recent years, and many operators deliberately avoid targeting them. Inland, the Glomma at Rånåsfoss and the lakes around Lillestrøm hold good predator fishing for pike, perch, zander and asp. Western Norway between Stavanger and Ålesund is fjord fishing in the strict sense: steep walls, deep water close to shore, coalfish and pollack as the staple species. The fjords are more sheltered than the open coast, which cuts down on lost days. Trøndelag, with Hitra and Frøya, combines both. Halibut sit on the sandbanks off the islands, while inland the Gaula, Orkla and Namsen count among the best-known salmon rivers in Europe. Nordland and Lofoten form the densest camp region in the country. The mix of sheltered sounds and steep edges allows trips even in poor weather, and between January and April the skrei — spawning cod migrating in from the Barents Sea — arrives on the coast. Troms and Finnmark are the extreme end. Sørøya, Havøysund and the coast up to the Russian border produce the largest halibut and coalfish, at the cost of the longest journey and the highest weather risk.

 

Target species and season

Cod can be caught year-round, peaking during the skrei season from January to April in the north. Coalfish feed hardest from June to September, when the shoals hold in open water. Halibut has a window of roughly May to October, with the best weeks in late summer. Ling and tusk sit deeper and are caught year-round, mainly in spring. Mackerel appear on the south coast from June. Salmon run into the rivers between June and August, sea trout are fished along the coast mainly in spring and autumn, and trout and char in the mountain lakes from June to September, once the snowmelt has passed.

 

Methods and tackle

At sea, jigging and pirking over deep water dominates, usually with 150 to 400 grams and heavier on strong tides. Halibut are fished with natural bait on the bottom or with large soft plastics on the drift, often over sand between 30 and 80 metres. Braid is standard given the depths. On the coast, a spinning rod and waders are enough for sea trout; in the salmon rivers, the two-handed rod is the norm. Light tackle in the 4- to 6-weight range covers the mountain lakes.

 

Rules you should know

Three points matter most for visiting anglers. First, export limits: only a restricted quantity of fish fillet may be taken out of the country, with guests of registered businesses allowed more than independent travellers. Separate rules apply to halibut. Second, mandatory disinfection: used tackle, waders and boats brought in from abroad must be disinfected and certified before being used in salmon-bearing waters. The reason is the parasite Gyrodactylus salaris. Third, freshwater licences: alongside the local fiskekort, a state fishing fee applies for salmon, sea trout and migratory char. Minimum sizes, closed seasons and quotas vary by river and region, and individual salmon rivers can be closed at short notice when run numbers are weak. 

 

Guided tours and fishing holidays

Anglers heading out on Norwegian water for the first time tend to underestimate two things: the depth, and how scattered the fish are. A guide with sonar and local knowledge shortens the search considerably, particularly for halibut. On Catch A Guide you'll find guided day trips, fishing camps with a boat and filleting house for those who prefer to head out on their own, and multi-day fishing trips with accommodation and a set programme. For Lofoten and Finnmark, be aware that the best camps are often fully booked a year ahead.

languages.title: Angeln in Spanien
languages.sub_title: Alles zum Thema Angeltouren, Angelguidings, Schonzeiten, Jahreszeiten & Infos zum Angeln in Spanien
languages.introduction: Angeln in Spanien ist eine Faszination für sich. Riesige Thunfische für der Mittelmeerküste Spaniens am Ebrodelta oder vor Mallorca, Mahi Mahi angeln, Welsangeln am Ebro, Forellenangeln in den Bergregionen, Schwarzbarsch angeln in den Stauseen, Karpfenangeln, super Zander & Barschangeln und die Liste könnte noch weitergehen. Um all diese Fischarten zu beangeln braucht man keinen Angelschein, sondern lediglich Erlaubniskarten. Die besten Regionen zum Angeln in Spanien sind die Costa del Sol, Costa Brava, Mequinenza, Pyrenäen, Extremadura, Ebro-Delta & Katalonien. Als Top-Gewässer gelten das Mittelmeer, der Atlantik, Ebro sowie Cinca & Segre. Dank des Mediterranen Klimas gilt Spanien als ganzjährig gut zu befischen, jedoch mit einer Hochphase für viele Fischarten im Frühjahr. Zum Angeln in Spanien am Meer sollte eine sehr robuste Ausrüstung mitgebracht werden. Für das Angeln auf Zander, Barsch, Wolfsbarsch oder Forellen reicht eine leichtere Spinnausrüstung. Das absolute Highilght für Spanien-Angler sind im Süßwasser der Wels und im Mittelmeer der Thunfisch. Für diese beiden Fischarten gibt es zahlreiche Anbeiter von Angeltouren. Auch Catch A Guide bietet eine große Auswahl an Angelguides, die ihre Tour hier darstellen und anbeiten.
languages.faq_title: Häufig gestellte Fragen zum Thema angeln in Spanien

languages.title: Fishing in Spain
languages.sub_title: All about tours, guides, closed seasons, best times & key info for fishing in Spain
languages.introduction: Fishing in Spain is a fascination of its own. Giant tuna off the Mediterranean coast around the Ebro Delta or Mallorca, mahi-mahi, catfish on the Ebro, trout in the mountains, largemouth bass in reservoirs, carp—plus excellent zander & perch: the list goes on. You don’t need a national fishing license, but you do need the relevant permits. Top areas include Costa del Sol, Costa Brava, Mequinenza, the Pyrenees, Extremadura, the Ebro Delta & Catalonia. Key waters are the Mediterranean, the Atlantic, and the rivers Ebro, Cinca & Segre. Thanks to the Mediterranean climate, Spain fishes well year-round, with a strong spring peak. For sea fishing, bring robust marine tackle; lighter spinning gear is fine for zander, bass (fresh/salt) and trout. Highlights for many are catfish in freshwater and tuna in the Mediterranean—there are numerous charter options, many listed on Catch A Guide.
languages.faq_title: Frequently asked questions about fishing in Spain

languages.title: Angeln in Kroatien
languages.sub_title: Alles zum Thema Angeltouren, Angelguidings, Schonzeiten, Jahreszeiten & Infos zum Angeln in Kroatien
languages.introduction: Kroatien steht ganz klar im Zeichen des Meeresangeln. Die Adriaküste mit den Hotspots Zadar, Split sowie der Insel Murter und Norddalmatien sind traumhafte Reviere zum Meeresangeln bzw. Big Game Fishing. Zu erwarten sind hier Thunfisch, Schwertfisch, Doraden, Wolfsbarsche und Makrelen. Das Angeln in Binnengewässern auf Hecht, Barsch, Zander, Forelle und Wels ist ebenfalls möglich, jedoch beschränken wir uns hier auf das Meeresangeln. Für das Angeln im Meer in Kroatien benötigt man eine Erlaubniskarte. Diese kostet von ca. 10€ je Tageskarte, bis zu ca. 40€ für eine Wochenkarte. Gerade für das Big Game Angeln gibt es etliche Anbieter für Angeltouren, die auf Catch A Guide gebucht werden können. Diese Angelguides haben das richtige Gerät und die besten Fangplätze, um die großen Meeresfische fangen zu können. Als beste Zeit des Jahres zum Angeln in Kroatien gelten Mai bis November, wobei die Hochsaison zwischen Juli und September liegt. Alles weitere zum Thema Angeltouren und Angeln in Kroatien findest du in diesem Beitrag.
languages.faq_title: Häufig gestellte Fragen zum Thema angeln in Kroatien

languages.title: Fishing in Croatia
languages.sub_title: All about tours, guides, seasons, waters & key info for fishing in Croatia
languages.introduction: Croatia is all about sea fishing. The Adriatic coast—Zadar, Split, the island of Murter and Northern Dalmatia—offers dream venues for big-game and inshore fishing. Expect tuna, swordfish, gilthead bream, European seabass and mackerel. Freshwater options (pike, perch, zander, trout, catfish) exist too, but here we focus on the sea. You need a permit for saltwater; day passes start ~€10, weekly around ~€40. There are plenty of charters for big game—bookable on Catch A Guide. These skippers have the right gear and prime spots. Best season: May–November, with peak from July–September.
